analysis.one_liner: Quadruples federal tobacco taxes and spends the money on health coverage for the uninsured.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Finance Committee without a vote in 1993, leaving the federal cigarette tax at about 24 cents a pack.
analysis.plain_summary: Senator Bill Bradley's bill would have raised the federal excise tax on cigarettes from $12 to $50 per thousand — roughly from 24 cents to $1 per pack — with similar increases on cigars, snuff, chewing and pipe tobacco. The new revenue would go into a Health Reform Trust Fund: 80% to pay for medical care and insurance for people who have none, and 20% for health education, quit-smoking programs, and payments to states that cut their own tobacco taxes to offset the federal increase. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People without health insurance, who would gain a dedicated funding stream for medical care and coverage; smokers who quit or never start, especially young people who are most sensitive to price; and the public at large through lower smoking rates. States that would have to cut their own tobacco taxes to offset the federal increase would receive compensation from the fund.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The uninsured, smokers who quit, and the public

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal cigarette tax from $12 to $50 per thousand — from roughly 24 cents to about $1 per pack — with proportionate increases on cigars, cigarette papers and tubes, snuff, chewing tobacco, and pipe tobacco.

Creates a Health Reform Trust Fund in the Treasury, funded by the net new revenue, with 80% dedicated to providing medical care and medical insurance to people without insurance and 20% to health education, smoking cessation programs, and payments to states required to reduce their own tobacco taxes because of the federal increase.

Imposes a one-time tax on tobacco inventory (floor stocks) held by wholesalers on January 1, 1994, so distributors cannot avoid the rate increase by stockpiling product before the higher rates take effect.

analysis.who_pays: Smokers, who would pay roughly $1 more per pack of cigarettes and more for other tobacco products; tobacco manufacturers and wholesalers, who would face sharply lower sales and a one-time tax on inventory; and tobacco growers and tobacco-dependent communities, who would bear the lost demand. Lower-income smokers would bear the largest share of the tax, since smoking is concentrated among them.

drawbacks.text: Tobacco taxes are regressive: the roughly $1-per-pack increase falls hardest on lower-income smokers who keep smoking, and the bill offers them no direct offset.

Spending from the trust fund is not automatic — the money is available only 'as provided by appropriation Acts,' so a future Congress could collect the tax and decline to appropriate the health coverage money.
Wholesalers and distributors face a one-time floor-stocks tax on all inventory held on January 1, 1994, and retailers would absorb reduced cigarette sales.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health payoff is real and large: a tax of this size reliably cuts smoking, especially among teenagers, and the bill dedicated the money to covering the uninsured. But the cost lands unevenly — on low-income smokers who keep smoking rather than on the industry's profits — and the coverage promise depended on future appropriations, so the bill's help for the uninsured was conditional while its cost to smokers was certain. A stronger design would have paired the tax with guaranteed spending and cessation support for the smokers paying it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on March 4, 1993 and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until that Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Senator Bill Bradley introduced the bill on March 4, 1993 with two cosponsors, one Republican and one Democrat.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day.
No further action was ever taken; the committee never held a markup or a vote, and the bill died when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers, wholesalers, and sellers were better off, since the quadrupled federal tobacco tax never took effect and smoking rates were not reduced by this measure. Smokers who kept smoking also avoided the higher prices.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Democrat and his two cosponsors split one Republican and one Democrat; because the bill never reached a vote, no roll call shows where the parties stood.

industries.note: A federal cigarette tax of $50 per thousand, up from $12, would have roughly quadrupled the tax on every pack and cut sales sharply across all tobacco products. The industry's interest in blocking the bill ran directly against the public health benefit of reduced smoking.

The bill imposed a one-time floor-stocks tax on all wholesale tobacco inventory held on January 1, 1994, with an exception only for retail-level stock, so distributors would have paid the higher rate on everything in their warehouses.
Higher prices would have reduced cigarette sales, cutting retail revenue, though retailers' existing stock was exempt from the floor-stocks tax.

Eighty percent of the new tax revenue was dedicated to providing medical care and insurance to the uninsured, which would have brought new patients and paying customers into the health system. The bill left the delivery mechanism unspecified, so insurers' share depended on later design.
